target.title: Lipreading with Long Short-Term Memory
target.venue: Not stated on the first page; arXiv [cs.CV] preprint

entries.text: The authors propose replacing the conventional visual-speech pipeline with a compact neural network trained end-to-end through its stacked feed-forward and recurrent layers.
entries.condition: Visual-only lipreading on GRID; feed-forward and LSTM layers form one network.

entries.text: The LSTM receives raw mouth images and learns features without a separate manually engineered feature-extraction stage.
entries.condition: The neural-network system; conventional comparator uses Eigenlips or HOG features.
entries.quote: Manual feature extraction is no longer required.

entries.text: The GRID corpus contains recordings from 34 speakers.
entries.condition: Full GRID audiovisual corpus; only speakers 1–19 were used in these experiments.

entries.text: Each GRID speaker says 1,000 sentences.
entries.condition: Full GRID corpus; corpus description, before unreadable-video exclusions in the experiment subset.

entries.text: The reported total recording duration of GRID is 28 hours.
entries.condition: Full GRID corpus, not the experiment's selected 19-speaker subset alone.

entries.text: GRID has a 51-word vocabulary arranged in six fixed sentence slots: command, color, preposition, letter, digit, and adverb.
entries.condition: Alternative counts are 4, 4, 4, 25, 10, and 4; letter W is excluded.

entries.text: Each GRID sentence lasts 3 seconds.
entries.condition: Fixed-structure GRID sentences, each spanning 75 video frames.

entries.text: The GRID videos run at 25 frames per second.
entries.condition: Fixed 3-second sentence recordings.

entries.text: A GRID sentence therefore spans 75 frames.
entries.condition: 3-second sentences at 25 fps.
entries.quote: Each sentences thus spans across 75 frames.

entries.text: The experiment used normal-quality 360 × 288 video converted to grayscale; unreadable videos were discarded, particularly for speaker 8.
entries.condition: The selected GRID recordings; speaker 8 is specifically mentioned as having unreadable videos.

entries.text: For each frame, the authors localized the face, used the LAB A channel and a Gaussian weighting to find the mouth center, then extracted a centered 40 × 40 grayscale patch, maximized contrast to [0,1], and standardized all dataset values.
entries.condition: Mathematica FindFaces; LAB A channel weighted by a Gaussian centered at 30% of image height (middle column), σ = 500 pixels; center of mass above 0.9; face area inflated by 1.5 and scaled to 128-pixel width; centered crop, grayscale, contrast remapped to [0,1], then dataset values standardized.
entries.quote: a window of 40 × 40 pixels with the mouth coordinates in the center was extracted.

entries.text: Frame-level GRID alignments were used to segment words, yielding 6,000 single-word items per speaker by the paper's stated count.
entries.condition: Computed in the paper as six words per each of 1,000 sentences; unreadable videos were discarded.
entries.quote:
The frame-
level alignments distributed with the corpus were used to ob-
tain word level segmentations of the video, causing the train-
ing dataset to consist of 6 · 1000 = 6000 single words per
speaker.

entries.text: Speakers 1–9 were the development set for parameter selection; speakers 10–19 were held back as the evaluation-speaker group.
entries.condition: The corpus contains 34 speakers, but the experiment uses speakers 1–19; evaluation IDs were not used for parameter setting.
entries.quote: speakers 1-9 form the development set that was used to determine the parameter settings

entries.text: Despite holding evaluation speaker IDs out of development, each classifier's training and test data came from the same speaker: the reported evaluation is speaker-dependent, not speaker-independent.
entries.condition: Applies to all systems; results are averaged over speakers.
entries.quote:
All exper-
iments are speaker-dependent, i.e. training and test data for
the classiﬁers were always taken from the same speaker.

entries.text: Within each speaker, data were randomly split into train, validation, and test sets; validation and test each contained five videos per word (255 samples each).
entries.unit: videos per word in each validation/test set; samples per set
entries.condition: 51-word GRID vocabulary; split performed separately for each speaker.
entries.quote:
The data for each speaker was randomly divided into train-
ing, validation, and test sets, where the latter two contain ﬁve
sample videos of each word, i.e. a total of 51 · 5 = 255 sam-
ples each.

entries.text: The authors note strong class imbalance in training: each letter appears 30 times per speaker while each color appears 240 times.
entries.unit: occurrences per speaker (each letter; each color)
entries.condition: Training data in the fixed-structure GRID corpus.

entries.text: The comparison systems were SVM classifiers paired with Eigenlips or HOG features.
entries.condition: Compared with the LSTM lipreader; HOG was selected after preliminary experiments.

entries.text: The selected Eigenlips representation retained 100 PCA components, with PCA fitted on training data.
entries.condition: Eigenlips + SVM baseline; setting determined using development speakers 1–9.

entries.text: The selected HOG cell size was 8.
entries.condition: HOG + SVM baseline; setting determined using development speakers 1–9.

entries.text: The best SVM setting used a linear kernel and a six-frame sequence feature vector; shorter sequences were repeated and longer ones averaged across neighboring frames.
entries.condition: SVM baselines; selected on development speakers 1–9.
entries.quote:
Best SVM
recognition results were obtained with a linear kernel at a se-
quence feature vector length of 6 frames.

entries.text: The selected LSTM network has one feed-forward layer, two recurrent LSTM layers with 128 units each, and a 51-unit softmax word classifier.
entries.unit: feed-forward layers; LSTM layers; units per LSTM layer; softmax classes
entries.condition: Best model selected on development speakers 1–9; input is a word's mouth-image sequence.
entries.quote:
The best LSTM lipreader consists of one feed-forward
layer followed by two recurrent LSTM layers, 128 units (neu-
rons / LSTM cells) each, and a softmax layer with 51 units
that perform the word classiﬁcation.

entries.text: LSTM training used learning rate 0.02, no momentum, and early stopping with a 10-epoch delay.
entries.unit: learning rate; epochs of early-stopping delay
entries.condition: Best LSTM configuration; momentum not used.

entries.text: Weights were initialized uniformly over [−0.05, 0.05].
entries.condition: Best LSTM configuration.

entries.text: Development-speaker Eigenlips + SVM word accuracy was 68.4% (SD 7.4%).
entries.condition: GRID visual-only word classification over 51 classes; development speakers 1–9; random per-speaker split; test set has 5 videos per word (255 samples per speaker); train/test are from the same speaker; results averaged over speakers; settings selected on these speakers; no LM reported; seed/repeats unreported.
entries.quote: Eigenlips + SVM 68.4% 7.4%

entries.text: Development-speaker HOG + SVM word accuracy was 71.1% (SD 6.7%).
entries.condition: GRID visual-only word classification over 51 classes; development speakers 1–9; random per-speaker split; test set has 5 videos per word (255 samples per speaker); train/test are from the same speaker; results averaged over speakers; settings selected on these speakers; no LM reported; seed/repeats unreported.

entries.text: Development-speaker LSTM word accuracy was 79.4% (SD 4.3%).
entries.condition: GRID visual-only word classification over 51 classes; development speakers 1–9; random per-speaker split; test set has 5 videos per word (255 samples per speaker); train/test are from the same speaker; results averaged over speakers; best LSTM settings selected on these speakers; no LM reported; seed/repeats unreported.

entries.text: Evaluation-speaker Eigenlips + SVM word accuracy was 70.6% (SD 4.2%).
entries.condition: GRID visual-only word classification over 51 classes; evaluation speakers 10–19; random per-speaker split; test set has 5 videos per word (255 samples per speaker); train/test are from the same speaker; hyperparameters optimized on speakers 1–9; results averaged over speakers; no LM reported; seed/repeats unreported.

entries.text: Evaluation-speaker HOG + SVM word accuracy was 71.3% (SD 4.3%).
entries.condition: GRID visual-only word classification over 51 classes; evaluation speakers 10–19; random per-speaker split; test set has 5 videos per word (255 samples per speaker); train/test are from the same speaker; hyperparameters optimized on speakers 1–9; results averaged over speakers; no LM reported; seed/repeats unreported.

entries.text: Evaluation-speaker LSTM word accuracy was 79.6% (SD 4.3%).
entries.condition: GRID visual-only word classification over 51 classes; evaluation speakers 10–19; random per-speaker split; test set has 5 videos per word (255 samples per speaker); train/test are from the same speaker; hyperparameters optimized on speakers 1–9; results averaged over speakers; no LM reported; seed/repeats unreported.

entries.text: The authors report an 11.6% accuracy improvement for LSTM over the best conventional system, HOG + SVM; the Table 1 values indicate relative gain rather than an 11.6-point increase (inference).
entries.condition: GRID visual-only word classification over 51 classes; evaluation speakers 10–19; per-speaker random split with 5 test videos per word (255 per speaker); train/test are from the same speaker; results averaged over speakers; comparator is HOG + SVM; no LM reported; seed/repeats unreported.
entries.quote: On the Evaluation Speakers 10– 19, the LSTM lipreader improves the accuracy by 11.6%, compared to the best conventional solution (HOG + SVM).

entries.text: The authors claim statistically significant improvement of LSTM over the conventional feature + SVM systems.
entries.condition: Word-level test accuracy comparisons in Table 1.

entries.text: The stated significance test was one-tailed with p = 0.05.
entries.condition: The paper does not provide the test statistic, degrees of freedom, or a detailed account of the observations compared; it is unclear whether p = 0.05 is an observed value or the cutoff.
entries.quote:
The LSTM lipreader yields statistically signiﬁcant
improvement (one-tailed t-test with p = 0.05) over the con-
ventional features combined with the SVM classiﬁer.

entries.text: On speaker 7, LSTM accuracy on letter classes was 69.8%.
entries.condition: Speaker 7 LSTM confusion matrix; letter subset of that speaker's 255-item word-level test set (5 videos per each of 51 classes); reported chance level 4%.

entries.text: The stated chance level for speaker 7's letter subset was 4%.
entries.condition: Speaker 7 LSTM test set; letter classes only.

entries.text: On speaker 7, LSTM accuracy on non-letter words was 93.4%.
entries.condition: Speaker 7 LSTM confusion matrix; non-letter subset of that speaker's 255-item word-level test set (5 videos per each of 51 classes); reported chance level 3.8%.

entries.text: The stated chance level for speaker 7's non-letter subset was 3.8%.
entries.condition: Speaker 7 LSTM test set; non-letter words only.

entries.text: The total LSTM word accuracy for speaker 7 was 82.0%.
entries.condition: Speaker 7 LSTM test set; all 51 GRID word classes, 5 videos per class (255 samples total).

entries.text: The authors report that errors concentrate on letters while longer words are recognized at close to 100% across speakers and setups.
entries.condition: Qualitative summary of confusion matrices; not a separate aggregate score.

entries.text: The authors attribute letter errors partly to visual confusability, including voiced/voiceless pairs such as p/b that may share visemes.
entries.condition: Visual-only recognition of GRID letter names.

entries.text: The authors note that letter clips can be only 3–4 frames long, leaving little visual evidence and making pronunciation sensitive to adjacent sounds.
entries.condition: GRID letter words; the paper states that adjacent-slot context does not help distinguish letters because sentence parts are statistically independent.

entries.text: The authors hypothesize that a dedicated sequence classifier such as an HMM would not substantially improve accuracy on this corpus; this was not experimentally tested in the reported results.
entries.condition: Inference based on the finding that a six-frame SVM feature vector covers available information for short letter clips.
entries.quote:
Taking this
observation into account, we hypothesize that a dedicated se-
quence classiﬁer like an HMM would not substantially im-
prove the classiﬁcation accuracy on this corpus.

entries.text: The authors say CNN substitutions were tried in experiments not described in the paper and did not improve the results.
entries.condition: CNN substituted for the fully connected feed-forward layer; no numeric results or protocol are supplied.
entries.quote:
The experiments, not described in this paper, also in-
cluded the highly popular CNNs instead of the fully con-
nected feed-forward layer, but the results did not improve.

entries.text: The authors leave experiments with larger images/CNNs and evaluation of a speaker-independent LSTM for future work; no speaker-independent result is reported here.
entries.condition: Current reported evaluations use speaker-dependent training and test data.
entries.quote: evaluation of a speaker-independent LSTM lipreader are the subject of future experiments.

entries.text: The system classifies individual word segments into 51 word classes; the reported metric is word accuracy, not sentence accuracy.
entries.condition: Word segments derived from GRID frame-level alignments; the acoustic corpus channel is excluded.

entries.text: Only visual mouth video was used; the audio component of GRID was excluded.
entries.condition: Visual-only word recognition from cropped grayscale mouth images.

entries.text: No random seed, number of repeated random splits, or repeated training runs is reported; the paper reports averages over speakers only.
entries.condition: Applies to random per-speaker train/validation/test partitions and stochastic neural-network training.
entries.quote: The data for each speaker was randomly divided

entries.text: The exact sample-selection procedure and random assignment of videos to each split are not reported beyond the per-word count.
entries.condition: Validation and test sets contain five videos per word; the paper does not identify which videos or whether the same split was used for all compared systems.

entries.text: The exact optimization criterion and whether validation rather than test results governed every parameter choice are not specified.
entries.condition: Parameters were optimized on speakers 1–9; each speaker had validation and test partitions.

entries.text: The paper says values across the complete dataset were standardized but does not define the standardization formula, axes, or fit scope (e.g. training-only versus full data).
entries.condition: Image preprocessing before evaluation; full-dataset standardization could include held-out data, but the exact implementation is not given.
entries.quote: all the values in the complete dataset were standardized.

entries.text: A chance-level comparator for the full 51-word task and the Table 1 averages is not reported; chance levels are given only for speaker 7's letter and non-letter subsets.
entries.condition: Overall word accuracy on the 51-class GRID vocabulary.

entries.text: The t-test's sample definition, pairing, statistic, degrees of freedom, and p-value interpretation are not stated beyond the reported p = 0.05.
entries.condition: Comparison of speaker-averaged word accuracy for LSTM with Eigenlips + SVM and HOG + SVM on the speaker-dependent test set.
entries.quote: The LSTM lipreader yields statistically signiﬁcant improvement (one-tailed t-test with p = 0.05)

entries.text: No explicit language-model or grammar-decoding stage is described; whether the fixed GRID sentence grammar constrains predictions at inference is not stated.
entries.condition: The described LSTM uses a 51-way softmax for word classification; sentence segments are evaluated as word classes.

entries.text: No user confirmation or rejection step is described or evaluated.
entries.condition: The paper reports offline word-classification accuracy, with no interactive user protocol.

entries.text: No user correction or adaptation mechanism is described or evaluated.
entries.condition: The paper reports offline word-classification accuracy, with no interactive user protocol.

entries.text: No real-time latency, throughput, user-facing deployment, or field evaluation is reported.
entries.condition: Evaluation is an offline, speaker-dependent test-set comparison.

entries.text: Sentence-level recognition accuracy is not reported; the results are word-level classification accuracy on aligned segments.
entries.condition: GRID's six-slot sentence structure is used to define word segments, but aggregate sentence accuracy is not evaluated.

entries.text: Word-level inference is evaluated on segments produced from corpus frame-level alignments; automatic word-boundary detection and continuous sentence decoding are not evaluated.

entries.text: CNN architecture: seven layers, four weighted layers (three convolutional and one fully connected), approximately 1.19×10^5 parameters, with a 40-way phoneme output.
entries.condition: Phoneme classification; six male speakers; images from 300 Japanese words; held-out image evaluation; seed and repeated fits not reported.

entries.text: CNN training maximized a multinomial logistic-regression objective, equivalent to average training-case log probability of the correct phoneme label.
entries.condition: Supervised phoneme classification; 40 labels; mouth-area images; word-recognition decoding is downstream GMM-HMM, not part of this objective.

entries.text: Approximately 1.23×10^5 mouth-image samples were shuffled; 5/6 were used for CNN training and the remainder for evaluation.
entries.condition: CNN phoneme evaluation; six speakers and 300 words; split is by shuffled images, with no subject- or vocabulary-held-out split specified. The separate word task trains on 216 words and tests on 84.

entries.text: A separate speaker-dependent CNN was prepared for each speaker after a preliminary experiment found lower precision with a single CNN over all six speakers.
entries.condition: Six male speakers; 300-word Japanese vocabulary; CNN phoneme task; seeds and repeated fits not reported.
entries.quote: Therefore, we prepared an independent CNN for each speaker.

entries.text: Image shuffling is reported, but no random seed, number of repeated fits, or run-to-run variability is reported.
entries.condition: CNN image-level train/evaluation split; six speakers; 300 words; word-level evaluation separately uses 84 held-out words; decoding uses GMM-HMM; seeds not stated.

entries.text: No validation-based model selection, epoch count, or stopping criterion is described; network structure parameters are said to be chosen empirically from prior studies.
entries.condition: CNN training; six speaker-specific models; validation set, seed, and early-stopping rule not stated.

entries.text: The recognition unit is an isolated word: CNN-derived phoneme-sequence features are decoded by left-to-right GMM-HMMs; continuous-stream decoding is not reported.
entries.condition: Test task: isolated word recognition; phoneme-sequence CNN features and left-to-right GMM-HMM decoding; no LM or seeds specified.
entries.quote: left-to-right GMM-HMMs are utilized for isolated word recognition.

entries.text: The audiovisual dataset contains 300 Japanese words from six speakers; visual input is recorded video processed as mouth-area image sequences.
entries.condition: Japanese audiovisual dataset; video-derived mouth-area images; 100-Hz visual recording, spatial ROI cropped and resized to 32×32 pixels.

entries.text: The 216 phonetically balanced word types are training data and the residual 84 word types are test data.
entries.condition: Word-level split: 216 phonetically-balanced training words and 84 residual test words.

entries.text: Evaluation uses 84 test words from the same speaker in a closed-speaker, open-vocabulary setup; monophone HMMs use 8, 16, or 32 GMM components.
entries.condition: Same-speaker test; 84 test words; monophone HMM with 8/16/32 GMM components; no LM or seed details reported.

entries.text: The paper does not specify how test-time word boundaries are supplied or detected. Its stated forced alignment assigns phoneme targets and is not identified as the test-word segmentation source.
entries.condition: Test inputs are isolated words; forced alignment is described for phoneme-label assignment, not for test-time word segmentation.

entries.text: Word segments are supplied to recognition as pre-cut isolated clips; the system does not detect word boundaries in continuous video.
entries.condition: Test input: individual word clips cut using MATLAB; speakers: CUAVE, 33 (17 male, 16 female); vocabulary: digits 0-9; decoding/LM: no language model reported; seeds: not reported.
entries.quote:
the individual words spoken by these speakers are cut using MATLAB
and are used as inputs.

entries.text: The task is isolated visual word recognition, classifying each word clip into one of ten digit classes (0-9).
entries.condition: CUAVE word clips; vocabulary: digits 0-9; decoding/LM: one-vs-one multiclass linear SVM, no language model reported; seeds: not reported.

entries.text: Evaluation is speaker-dependent: training and test data come from the same speaker, repeated across all 33 speakers.
entries.condition: Test set: same-speaker held-out data; speakers: 33; vocabulary: digits 0-9; decoding/LM: linear SVM, no language model reported; seeds: not reported.

the training
of the system was performed using training data from a single speaker and the testing data from the

entries.condition: CUAVE; test set: 5-fold validation within each speaker (50 word vectors per speaker); speakers: 33, speaker-dependent; vocabulary: digits 0-9; decoding/LM: one-vs-one linear SVM, no language model reported; seeds: not reported.

entries.text: The best single-speaker visual system uses an 84-dimensional hand-engineered vector: 36 LGE geometric features plus 6 intensity features and their deltas, not raw pixels or PCA/DCT coefficients.
entries.condition: LGE plus intensity features; limited-vocabulary digit recognition

entries.text: The visual word recognizer maps its feature sequence with HMMs, including digit models and silence/pause models; the best word-level result is not produced by a recurrent neural classifier.
entries.condition: Limited-vocabulary connected-digit recognition
entries.quote: All of the lipreading experiments performed during this research employed Hidden Markov Models as the recognition engine.

entries.text: A Jordan recurrent network is used for a separate visual speech/silence onset-offset task, not for the word-level digit recognizer.
entries.condition: Frame-level speech activity detection

entries.text: An Elman hierarchical recurrent network is used for the separate vowel/consonant frame-classification task; no LSTM or stochastic/diffusion recurrent word recognizer is reported.
entries.condition: Frame-level vowel/consonant discrimination
entries.quote: An extension to the JNN, the Elman Hierarchical Neural Network, is used in the vowel/consonant discrimination experiments described further on in this chapter.

entries.text: Feature extraction is a separate preprocessing step: LGE geometry and intensity features are computed from video before the temporal HMM classifier; there is no joint end-to-end back-propagation training.
entries.condition: Visual-only limited-vocabulary experiments
entries.quote: Both sets were then processed in order to extract geometric and intensity related features from the video sequences following the model described in Chapter 4.

entries.text: The recognition unit is a digit in connected digit strings, with a 10-digit vocabulary and grammar constraints; this is not isolated-word recognition or unrestricted natural continuous speech.
entries.condition: Connected strings; constrained or unconstrained digit grammar

entries.text: The best result is speaker-dependent: training and test recordings are from the same single native Dutch female speaker.
entries.condition: One female speaker; random split into digit-set training and test data

entries.text: Best visual-only word accuracy is 81.1% with constrained grammar and LGE-plus-intensity features; the corresponding correct-digit rate is 86.7%.
entries.condition: One speaker; connected digits; LGE+intensity; constrained grammar

entries.text: Classifier input is a cropped mouth ROI rescaled to 60 × 80 pixels and PCA-whitened to 32 dimensions, rather than geometric lip features.
entries.condition: Visual preprocessing

entries.text: The visual input uses 4 contiguous video frames and includes temporal derivatives over the reduced vector.
entries.condition: Visual input window

entries.text: A video-only deep autoencoder learns the visual representation; a linear SVM maps the resulting features to speech classes. No recurrent model (including Elman, Jordan, PRNN, stochastic/diffusion recurrent nets, or LSTM) is reported.
entries.condition: Visual-only classification

entries.text: Feature extraction is learned separately: deep autoencoders are trained on unlabeled data, then their representations are used for supervised SVM classification, not jointly trained end-to-end with a temporal classifier.
entries.value: separate unsupervised feature learning and supervised classification
entries.condition: Deep autoencoder features followed by linear SVM
entries.quote: All deep autoencoder models were trained with all available unlabeled audio and video data.

entries.text: AVLetters is isolated-letter recognition (A–Z, 26 classes; 10 speakers, 3 repetitions). The cited third-test protocol is reported, but its speaker-dependent versus speaker-independent split is not specified.
entries.condition: AVLetters visual-only lipreading

entries.text: CUAVE evaluates isolated digits 0–9 (10 classes; normal portion, 36 speakers, 5 repetitions per digit) speaker-independently, with even-numbered speakers for training and odd-numbered speakers for testing.
entries.condition: CUAVE normal portion; speaker-independent split
entries.quote: We evaluated digit classiﬁcation on the CUAVE dataset in a speaker independent setting.
entries.loc: Section 4.2, Datasets and Task; Table 1(b) note

entries.text: On the AVLetters letter task, the video-only deep autoencoder scores 64.4% ± 2.4%.
entries.condition: AVLetters visual-only letter recognition

entries.text: The classifier uses geometric lip-contour shape features, not raw or downsampled mouth-region pixels; shape is represented by PCA eigenvectors, scale, and temporal deltas.
entries.unit: 10 shape eigenvectors plus scale and deltas
entries.condition: per still frame

entries.text: The visual representation also includes contour-sampled gray-level intensity profiles, reduced by PCA and augmented with temporal deltas (40 intensity parameters per frame).
entries.condition: shape-and-intensity configuration

entries.text: Feature extraction is separate from classifier training: contours/PCA descriptors are supplied as pre-extracted inputs, and the paper does not describe joint end-to-end back-propagation through the visual front end and temporal model.
entries.value: fixed/pre-extracted features; no joint end-to-end training reported
entries.condition: lip-contour features feed the diffusion networks
entries.quote:
in this experiment we use lip contours extracted
from the database [7, 8, 6].

entries.text: The temporal model is a stochastic recurrent neural network called a diffusion network, with continuous-state SDE dynamics; no Elman, Jordan, partially recurrent, or LSTM model is reported.
entries.condition: visual speech sequence recognition

entries.text: Speech classes are scored by a bank of four class-specific diffusion networks, one per word, using the likelihood of each observed lip-contour trajectory.
entries.condition: one network per word class
entries.quote:
The distributions of lip-contour
trajectories were modeled using a bank of 4 diffusion
networks, one per word to be recognized.

entries.text: The recognition unit is an individual digit-word utterance: a four-class isolated-word task (one, two, three, four), not continuous multiword speech.
entries.condition: individual Tulips1 utterances

entries.text: Evaluation is speaker-independent: models are tested on a held-out subject after training on the other subjects (leave-one-subject-out jackknife).
entries.condition: generalization to an unseen speaker
entries.quote:
Networks were evaluated in
terms of generalization to new speakers.

entries.text: The best automatic visual-only result is 91.7% with the diffusion network using both shape and intensity features.
entries.condition: Tulips1; diffusion (shape and intensity); speaker-independent generalization

entries.text: Baseline visual input is a 384-dimensional vector of low-pass-filtered, 24x16 downsampled grayscale lip pixels, histogram-normalized to [-1,1].
entries.condition: Direct gray-level input
entries.quote: The resulting sequence of 384-dimensional “normalized pixel vectors” (one vector for each lip image frame) is then used as the input to the recognition algorithm.

entries.text: The paper also tests image-derived PCA (32 coefficients), supervised LDA (32), and DFT-ring coefficients (29); it reports no geometric lip-feature representation.
entries.condition: Alternative visual inputs

entries.text: The visual path is a modular MS-TDNN producing activations for 42 visual viseme states. The described model uses time-delay processing; the paper does not describe a recurrent network.
entries.condition: Visual-only recognizer
entries.quote: In the basic system a modular Multi-State Time Delay Neural Network (MS-TDNN) [5] is used to perform the recognition.

entries.text: Temporal sequence decoding uses a DTW path through the phone states; time is therefore handled by TDNN delays and state-path alignment, rather than recurrent state.
entries.condition: Letter-sequence recognition
entries.quote: a one'stage DTW algorithm finds the optimal path through the phone states that decodes the recognized letter sequence.

entries.text: Network weights are trained by back-propagation. Raw pixels allow internal representations to be learned by the network; PCA/LDA/DFT are separate input transformations. The paper reports state-level outputs plus DTW decoding, not a word-level end-to-end objective.
entries.value: Back-propagation; no word-level end-to-end objective reported
entries.condition: Visual branch and alternative feature representations
entries.quote: The weights in the parallel networks are trained by backpropagation.
entries.loc: Section 2.1, Fundamental Design; Section 2.2, Visual Data Representation

entries.text: The task is continuous spelling of names and nonsense letter sequences of arbitrary length over the German alphabet, a small, highly confusable vocabulary; a reported “word” is one pronounced letter.
entries.value: Continuous German-alphabet letter spelling; one letter per recognition unit
entries.condition: Names and nonsense sequences; arbitrary length
entries.quote: It is designed to recognize continuously spelled names and nonsense letter sequences of arbitrary length using the German alphabet.

entries.text: Evaluation is speaker-dependent: the 200 sequences were split into 170 training, 15 cross-validation, and 15 test sequences from one male speaker.
entries.condition: Within-speaker split
entries.quote: visual speech data from one (male) speaker.

entries.text: The authors aim to replace the whole visual speech recognition pipeline with one compact neural network, with raw mouth images as input, in contrast to feature-based systems.

questions.q: Does the reported 79.6% establish speaker-independent lipreading?
questions.answer: No. Speakers 10–19 were held out for parameter selection, but each classifier's training and test data came from the same speaker; speaker-independent evaluation is explicitly left for future work.
They report 11.6%; Table 1's 79.6% versus 71.3% indicates a relative gain rather than an 11.6-percentage-point increase (inference). The comparator is HOG + SVM.

questions.q: Which implementation and evaluation details limit reproducibility?
questions.answer: The paper omits random seeds and repeat counts, exact split assignments, the full validation/model-selection criterion, standardization details, and several t-test details; no linked author code repository is provided.

questions.q: Which priors before 2015-07 use a recurrent or time-delay network on lip input, and on what input (pixels or extracted features), trained jointly or separately?
questions.answer: Movellan and Mineiro 1999: diffusion networks over lip-contour PCA features (v1-v4). Wojdel 2003: Jordan/Elman networks for frame tasks, HMM words, extracted features (d2-d5). Duchnowski et al. 1994: MS-TDNN on 384 gray-level pixel values, back-propagation, DTW (u1-u5). Ngiam 2011 and Noda 2014: features learned separately (g4, c4, c7).
